title: Three Qubits Sharing a Single Josephson Junction
hook: Superconducting processors usually give each qubit its own hardware. The 'multiunimon' packs three into one junction — and does three-qubit gates natively, in the time a single-qubit gate takes.
key_points: Most quantum algorithms compile down to one- and two-qubit gates; native multi-qubit gates can cut circuit depth sharply on noisy hardware.
The multiunimon is a superconducting multimode circuit encoding several qubits in one Josephson junction embedded in a coplanar waveguide.
It inherits the unimon qubit's traits: high anharmonicity, full protection from low-frequency charge noise, partial protection from flux noise.
Simulating a three-qubit device with Josephson-to-inductive energy ratio above 1, all twelve controlled-controlled-NOT gates reached a mean fidelity of 99.5%.
The pulses were simple sine-squared shapes of length comparable to a single-qubit gate.
Performance was limited by incoherent errors dominated by dielectric loss — a materials problem, not a design one.
content_html: A quantum algorithm is normally compiled into a long sequence of one- and two-qubit gates. On noisy hardware, length is the enemy: every extra layer is another chance for an error. That makes native multi-qubit gates — operations that act on three qubits at once, in hardware — an attractive shortcut, if a circuit can be built to support them.
extra_html: Sasu Tuohino, Mikko Möttönen and Matti Silveri propose the multiunimon: a superconducting multimode circuit that encodes multiple qubits in a device containing a single Josephson junction embedded in a coplanar waveguide structure. It is a close relative of the unimon qubit and inherits its useful properties — high anharmonicity, full protection against low-frequency charge noise, and partial protection against flux noise. Designing a three-qubit version with the Josephson-to-inductive energy ratio above unity, and using a leakage-aware encoding of the computational states, the authors simulate all twelve distinct controlled-controlled-NOT gates and obtain a mean fidelity of 99.5%. The pulses are plain sine-squared shapes, no longer than a typical single-qubit gate. The remaining error budget is dominated by dielectric loss — an incoherent, materials-driven limit, which the authors argue leaves clear headroom as fabrication improves.

related.title: Qubits and Quantum Computing
related.hook: A normal bit is a 0 or a 1. A qubit can be both at once — and linking many of them lets a quantum computer explore a staggering number of possibilities together.

related.title: A Silicon Qubit Gate That Misfires Once in a Million Tries
related.hook: Spin qubits in silicon just crossed 99.999% single-gate fidelity — and getting there meant discovering that some of the field's benchmark numbers were partly artefacts.

related.title: Superconductivity: Electricity with Zero Resistance
related.hook: Cool certain materials cold enough and their electrical resistance vanishes completely. A current set flowing in a loop would, in principle, circle forever without fading.

related.title: First-Ever Coherent Control of a Majorana Qubit
related.hook: Majorana zero modes promise qubits that resist noise almost by design. A Delft-led team just demonstrated the first coherent control of one, a step toward fault-tolerant quantum computers.

flashcards.prompt: Why would native multi-qubit gates help a noisy quantum processor?
flashcards.back_html: Algorithms normally decompose into long chains of one- and two-qubit gates. Doing a three-qubit operation directly cuts circuit depth, giving errors less time to accumulate.

flashcards.prompt: What is unusual about the multiunimon's hardware layout?

choices.text: It encodes multiple qubits in a single Josephson junction embedded in a coplanar waveguide
It uses no Josephson junctions at all
It stores each qubit in a separate cryostat

flashcards.explanation_html: It is a multimode circuit: several modes of one junction-and-waveguide structure carry the qubits, inheriting the unimon's charge-noise protection and high anharmonicity.

flashcards.prompt: What limited the simulated 99.5% mean CCNOT fidelity?
flashcards.back_html: Incoherent errors dominated by dielectric loss — a materials-quality limitation rather than a flaw in the gate scheme, so better materials should push fidelity up.
